The Story of Seeing Virtues in Others

I bow to Lord Jina, who is worshipped by the gods of heaven, and I write the story of one who, instead of seeing others' faults, takes their virtues.

One day, Indra, the king of Saudharm heaven, was overcome with love of dharma and was praising virtuous souls in his assembly. At that time he said, 'That person, that great soul, whose heart is so generous that, paying no attention to the many faults in others, he strives to magnify even the small virtues present in them — whose attention is focused only on taking virtues — that person, that great soul, is the best in the world, and his birth too is successful.'

Hearing Indra praise the virtue-taking person in this way, a whimsical god asked him, 'O king of gods, as you have praised the virtue-taking person just now, is there any such fortunate soul on earth?' Indra replied, 'Yes, there is — and that is the last Vasudev, Shrikrishna, lord of Dwaraka.' Hearing this, that god immediately came to earth.

At this time, Shrikrishna was going to see Lord Neminath. To test him, the god took the form of a dead dog and lay on the path. A terrible stench emanated from its body. Coming and going had become difficult because of it. Unable to bear this unbearable stench, all of Shrikrishna's companions fled. At that moment, the god took the form of another Brahmin and came to Shrikrishna and began to criticise the dog, pointing out its faults.

Shrikrishna listened to all his words and then said, 'Ah! Look, how pure and beautiful is the row of teeth of this dog, like crystal!' Shrikrishna, paying no attention to the dog's other faults, its stench, etc., actually praised only its teeth — the small good part that remained in it.

Seeing Shrikrishna's such generous mind even toward an animal, the god was very pleased. He then revealed his true form, told Shrikrishna the whole story, gave him proper honour and respect, and returned to his place.

In the same way, other devotees of Lord Jina, worthy souls, should also strive to abandon others' faults and take their virtues with love for the sake of happiness. Only thus can they be called discerning and worthy of praise.

This story teaches the supreme virtue of seeing the good in others rather than focusing on their faults. Even Shrikrishna, when faced with a dead dog's corpse, chose to praise its beautiful teeth rather than complain about the stench. The wise should cultivate this generous vision — focusing on others' virtues rather than their faults. This is the mark of a truly noble soul.
